lines.note: Minikui sahoo ja describes an ugly or objectionable manner. The damaged f in ſafôgia is read with the preceding page's Safô, not the draft's t; initial &c. continues that definition.
The manner is bad and offensive to the eye. This completes the Portuguese translation of minikui sahoo ja.
Sahodo means to that extent or as much as that; the gloss supplies the demonstrative degree comparison.
Sagari gives the intransitive forms for lowering or descending. Ato ni sagaru introduces the sense of moving or remaining behind.

runs.text: Vir, ou ficar de tras. ¶ Item, Em-

lines.note: The divided sagaru is completed and glossed as coming or staying behind; another sense, deterioration, begins in Em-.
Te ga sagaru illustrates worsening skill or handwriting. The gloss completes empeyorar, retaining the historical spelling.

runs.text: Amão, ou letra do eſcriuão vai empeyoran-

lines.note: The writer's hand or script is deteriorating. Amão remains close-set as supplied, and empeyorando continues below.
Ne ga sagaru means that the price falls. The scan reads Abater, not Abaper; the merchandise is specified next.
The price explanation ends, then fish or meat is said to sagaru. The next lines explain this as beginning to spoil.

runs.text: Eſtar o peixe, ou carne hum pouco ſentida, ou

lines.note: The fish or meat is slightly tainted. Sentida is read in this food-spoilage context, not in the emotional sense of hurt.
This completes the description of food showing the beginnings of decay, the final illustrated sense of sagaru here.
Sagaribara no ko denotes a child born outside the recognized marriage; the close-set Filhoillegitimo is retained, and molher is divided.

runs.text: lher que não he a propria.

lines.note: The mother is described as someone other than the man's own wife. Final B. is upright and marks the register, not part of the italic sentence.

runs.text: Modo de tanger nos autos, ou dan-

lines.note: Sagariha names a musical manner used in plays or dances. Its performance occasion is explained in the following rows.

runs.text: ças atempo que ſayem algũas figuras, ou mui-

lines.note: The music accompanies figures coming out in the performance, either some or many together. Atempo retains the source's close spacing.
This completes muitas juntas, many figures together. The small terminal mark is a comma in the scan, not the draft's full stop.
Sagashi, sagasu, sagaita means searching or investigating carefully; the supplied historical -aita form is not modernized to -ashita.
The Benkei quotation begins amari no kanashi-, excessive sorrow. The Portuguese diligence gloss ends before this example.

runs.text: ſani voiuo acacayexi fita ſagaxini ſagai-

lines.note: The quotation continues with sorrow, overturning the carrier or box, and searching intently. The damaged first c of acacayexi is retained provisionally; the Portuguese supplies the overturning sense. Final ſagai- belongs with tareba below.
The quotation ends in sagaitareba. Tog. is an upright citation label; the Portuguese translation begins with Benkei's great sorrow.

runs.text: triſteza reuoluendo a caxa de cima pera baixo,

lines.note: The translation describes turning the box upside down in sorrow, clarifying the action in the Japanese quotation.
Benkei does nothing but search. The separated ſe não is retained as historical phrasing rather than modernized to senão.
The noun sagashi denotes searching and rummaging. Yasa- begins yasagashi, a search of a house, on the next line.
Yasagashi wo suru means searching the house. This completes both the divided Japanese example and its Portuguese explanation.
Sagashidashi means bringing something out by feeling or searching for it. The Portuguese searching phrase continues across the line break.
Tirar fora completes the action of extracting the thing found by touch or search, not merely looking for it.
Sagashii describes a steep place difficult to ascend. Its physical-terrain sense is distinct from the preceding searching verbs.
Sagashii yama is a steep mountain. The Portuguese translation divides ingreme at the physical right edge.
The mountain is steep and rugged. This completes the terrain example without adding any further Japanese word.
The separately printed sagashi idashi repeats the extraction-by-search sense; its spacing is preserved rather than assimilated to Sagaxidaxi above.
This again completes the explanation as taking something out after finding it by touch or search.
Sagashimawashi means searching around in different places. Its printed -aita principal part follows the historical morphology described in the supplied notes.
The search is carried out in various places. Printed per is retained rather than modernized to por.
Sage gives transitive forms for lowering something. Atama- begins the example of lowering one's head.
Atama wo saguru means lowering the head in humility. The historical saguru form is preserved rather than replaced with modern sageru.
The head is lowered in submission or for another reason. The supplied irregular word spacing is retained; Fi- begins hito in the next example.
Hito wo saguru means humbling or bringing another person low. The scan reads abaixar rather than the draft's abuixar.
The object is another person. This closes the figurative humbling example before the compound entries that follow.
Sagegiri is a manner of cutting downward. The scan supplies the i in guiri missing from the draft's guri.
Sage iyashime means despising or lowering another. The Portuguese abater is divided after its initial a-.
The action is directed against another person, completing the gloss of contempt or humiliation.
Sagesumi means dropping a plumb or line to test alignment. The following carpentry explanation establishes the concrete sense.

runs.text: como fazem os carpinteiros pera ver ſe esta di-

lines.note: Carpenters use the line to see whether something is straight. The supplied esta is retained without adding an accent from modern spelling.
Iye wo sagesumu illustrates checking a house by a line. The upright e in Iyeuo corrects the draft's c and agrees with the house gloss.

runs.text: Deitando a linha ver ſe està a caſa direita.

lines.note: The translation explicitly tests whether the house is straight. The worn accented està is retained with the supplied grave reading.
The figurative application is judging or assessing a person. The scan supports Permet., initial long s in ſagueſumu, and italic Olhar; the explanation continues in column 2.

runs.text: ou conſiderar a alguem, ou ponderar ſuas qua-

lines.note: The figurative sagesumu explanation continues from column 1: considering a person and weighing that person's qualities.

runs.text: lidades, ou interior, &c. às vezes ſe toma por

lines.note: The assessment concerns qualities or inner character; the dictionary then introduces a sometimes disparaging application.

runs.text: ver, & penetrar alguẽ tẽdo delle menos cõceito.

lines.note: The person is scrutinized while held in low esteem. The scan restores cõceito and the continuous penetrar, rather than the draft's defective forms.
The noun sagesumi is a conjecture or estimate. The scan reads Conjetura without the draft's extra i; the example continues below.
Sagesumi wo suru means conjecturing or weighing something. Conjeturar likewise lacks the inserted i in the draft.

runs.text: Cordam que està dependurado na bai-

lines.note: Sageo is the cord hanging from a sword scabbard. The headword has u rather than n, and enlargement shows the grave accent in està; bainha is divided.
This completes the scabbard description for the swords called catanas. It ends the sageo entry before the independently printed sagezaya row omitted by the draft.

runs.text: Bainha de facas que ſe traz de pẽ-

lines.note: Sagezaya is a knife sheath worn hanging. This complete physical row was missing from the draft; its pẽ- continues with durada in the retained next row.
Durada completes the hanging-sheath description begun in the restored sagezaya row. It must not be attached to the preceding sageo entry.
Sagezuchi is a suspended hammer or pestle. The close-set dependuradode is retained, and the next row describes its support and use.

runs.text: hum bambu comprido, com que batem papel.

lines.note: The implement hangs from a long bamboo and is used to beat paper. The scan reads bambu, not the draft's bamhu.
Sagi is glossed as a heron. The entry is a bird name, distinct from the following homonymous verbal form.
This sagi is labelled a defective verb and illustrated with melons becoming past their prime. Defect. replaces the draft's broken de ſec.

runs.text: Estarem ja acabados os melões, ou ter

lines.note: The divided urisagita is completed; the Portuguese says the melons are already finished or have lost their vigor.
The explanation of melons past their prime ends, and sagiuri introduces the corresponding noun for poor late-season melons.

runs.text: lões ruins, e magrentos, depois de paſſar ja o

lines.note: These are inferior, lean melons after their best time has passed. The source retains e rather than replacing it with an ampersand.
The season and vigor of the melons have passed. Final X. is an upright regional-usage label, not part of the italic gloss.

runs.text: Ceremonia gentilica que ſe faz no

lines.note: Sagichoo names a non-Christian ceremony described by the dictionary. The following rows specify its New Year setting and bonfire.
Shooguachi, the New Year period, is embedded in the Portuguese description. A bonfire is made in front of a house.

runs.text: caſa em que queimão varias couſas.

lines.note: Various things are burned in that bonfire. This completes the source's description without adding details of later festival practice.
Sageoo is explained as nasu waza and glossed as deeds, life, or conduct. The scan supports final ô rather than the draft's ǒ.
Sagiuri refers back to the earlier sagi entry on overripe melons. The initial is S, not B; Sagui is a Japanese cross-reference within Latin apparatus.
Sagoromo is equated with koromo, clothing. Final P. is upright and labels poetic usage rather than extending the italic definition.
Saguri gives the forms for feeling or touching by hand. The gloss emphasizes tactile probing, not the broader searching sense of sagashi.
Sai means skill or knowledge; sai aru hito is a person possessing it. The Portuguese Homem is divided at the margin.
This completes the description of a person with knowledge and practical skill, translating sai aru hito.
This sai is a side dish of fish, meat, vegetables, or similar food. The scan reads ti-, beginning tirando, not the draft's tu-.
Tirando excludes rice and shiru from this category of dishes. Xiru is the Japanese soup term embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
A third sai means dice; sai wo utsu is playing or casting them. The source's Iugar is retained as printed.
Casting the dice completes the verbal example. The short row belongs to the dice sense, not the following marital term.
Saiai is the union of husband and wife. The gloss itself does not require adding a narrower interpretation to the transcription.
Saiai suru gives the verbal construction for that marital union. There is no separate Portuguese translation printed on this row.
Saiban means having charge or administration of something here, rather than assuming its modern judicial sense.
Ie no saiban wo suru illustrates administering a household. The Portuguese governar begins with Go- at the line end.
This completes governar a casa, governing or managing the house, confirming the administrative sense of saiban.
Saibitsu is a square chest for provisions. The scan shows mata- at the right edge; the draft's final r was a misread continuation mark.
Lotagem completes matalotagem, provisions or supplies. It is not an independent Portuguese word or a new entry.
Saibon is explained as futatabi okasu, committing an offense again. The Portuguese segunda is divided as ſegun-, not the draft's ſegur.
The gloss says a second time. Final S. is an upright written-usage label and is kept outside the italic explanation.
Saibon saige describes something or someone very lowly or base. The following example applies it specifically to a person.
Saibon, saige no hito is the personal example of a low or base man. The small raised mark after Ho is retained as a worn hyphen; mem completes homem below.
The person is lowly and base. This completes the divided Homem and its modifiers.

runs.text: Hũa certa ſeita de Bonzos Ienxus.

lines.note: Saika is identified as a particular sect among the monks called Ienxus. The historical sect description is retained without imposing a modern classification.
Saikaku means ingenuity or prudence. The scan restores Induſtria; the repeated Japanese example divides Sai and cacu without a supplied hyphen.
Saikaku wo megurasu means exercising ingenuity. The scan supports cacuuo with the object particle uo, not the draft's cacuno.
Invention completes the explanation of using one's ingenuity. This is the close of the example, not a separate sense.
Saikakusha is a knowledgeable and resourceful person. The worn Portuguese adjective is read as induſtrioſo, replacing the draft's malformed indauſtioſo.
